subject: Banking
title: Temples as the First Banks
description: A quick, practical guide to Temples as the First Banks.

hook.text: Ancient Mesopotamian temples stored grain and silver for citizens. Priests kept ledgers.

buildup.text: Farmers deposited harvests for safekeeping. Merchants borrowed against stored goods. Temples charged fees for both.

discovery.text: These temples invented deposit-taking, lending, and record-keeping.

twist.text: Temples lent at interest rates of 20-33%. Modern credit cards look cheap compared to ancient Sumerian lending.

climax.text: Banking was born from the need to store value safely and lend it profitably. That formula has never changed.

punchline.text: First banks were temples. 4,000 years later, the model still works.

quiz.question: Where were the earliest known banks?

details.summary: Ancient temples in Mesopotamia, Greece, and Rome served as the world's first banks, storing valuables, making loans, and managing wealth. Their sacred status provided the security and trust that financial transactions require.
details.whyItMatters: Banking began not in counting houses but in sacred spaces. The earliest financial institutions relied on religious authority for the trust that modern banks build through regulation and insurance.
takeaways: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the ancient world's major banks
Temples stored grain, gold, and other valuables as deposits
Sacred status deterred theft and provided the trust needed for banking

faq.question: Why were temples the first institutions to offer banking?
faq.answer: Temples were the most secure and trusted buildings in ancient cities. Their religious authority deterred robbery and provided moral enforcement of contracts. People trusted temples with valuables in a way they would not trust private individuals.

faq.question: What banking services did ancient temples offer?
faq.answer: Temples stored deposits of grain, gold, and other valuables. They made loans to farmers and merchants, often charging interest. Some temples also facilitated long-distance trade by issuing letters that could be redeemed at other temples.
